title: The Synoptic Problem
lead: Matthew, Mark and Luke share much of their material, often word for word and in the same order. The Synoptic problem asks how: who used whom, and whether a lost source ("Q") lies behind the sayings that Matthew and Luke share but Mark lacks.

sections.b: About 90 percent of Mark appears in Matthew, and about half of it in Luke, often in the same words and order. Matthew and Luke also share about 230 verses that Mark does not have, mostly sayings of Jesus (the Lord's Prayer, the Beatitudes, John the Baptist's preaching, the testing in the wilderness). Where Matthew and Luke both run parallel to Mark, they rarely agree with each other against him in the order of events. Each Gospel also has material of its own, such as Matthew's magi and Luke's shepherds. There are also the "minor agreements": small places where Matthew and Luke agree in wording against Mark in passages all three share (for example Matthew 26:68 and Luke 22:64, "Who struck you?"). Supporters of the Farrer view count them as the strongest evidence that Luke knew Matthew; defenders of Q explain them as coincidence, shared oral tradition or later copying.
sections.refs: Matthew 3:7–10; Luke 3:7–9; Matthew 4:1–11; Mark 1:12–13; Luke 4:1–13; Matthew 6:9–13; Luke 11:2–4; Matthew 26:68; Luke 22:64; Mark 14:65

sections.b: The two-source hypothesis (the view of most scholars since B. H. Streeter's The Four Gospels, 1924): Mark wrote first; Matthew and Luke each used Mark and, separately, a lost collection of sayings called Q (German Quelle, "source"). The Farrer hypothesis (Austin Farrer, Michael Goulder, Mark Goodacre): Mark first, Matthew used Mark, and Luke used both, so there is no need for Q. The Griesbach or two-Gospel hypothesis (J. J. Griesbach in 1789, revived by William Farmer in 1964): Matthew first, then Luke, and Mark combined them. Matthean priority in its traditional form, as in Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels): the canonical order is the order of writing, Matthew first. Some scholars add oral tradition and memory to any of these models.

If Matthew used Mark, then the places where Matthew changes Mark show what Matthew wanted to stress: Jesus' fulfillment of Scripture, his teaching, the church and the law. If Matthew was first, the same differences show what Mark and Luke left out or simplified. The site's notes point out such differences without assuming one answer.
